triage.question: A check of a Java build (Gradle: compile, tests, coverage, Checkstyle, PMD, SpotBugs) failed on a branch that a developer is working on. Judge how much reasoning and how many edits a fix needs, not how scary the message looks. Decide by: how many files and classes the cause touches, whether the cause is stated in the message or has to be found, whether it is deterministic, and whether it is a mechanical edit or a design decision. Many failures with one shared cause are as hard as that cause. Pick the one level that fits best.

trivial.describe: Mechanical, no judgement: formatting, an unused import, a missing license header, trailing whitespace. One obvious edit, usually in one place, nothing to investigate.

easy.describe: A small, obvious fix in one file: a missing semicolon or bracket, a misspelled name or package, a missing import, a missing javadoc. The error message names the exact line and the fix.

simple.describe: A compile or style error confined to one or two files that needs a small understanding of the code: a changed return type or parameter at a few call sites, a method that is too complex to pass the analyzer, an incompatible type, a possible null path.

moderate.describe: One failing test or one runtime error in one class whose cause is visible in the message: a wrong expected value, a null pointer or index out of bounds at a named line, a wrong status code. Reading one class and its test is enough.

average.describe: A failure that needs reading and changing a few classes together, or adding tests: two related test classes that disagree, a coverage threshold missed, a serialization or mapping change that touches a few classes and their tests.

hard.describe: A logic or design bug that spans several classes or modules: many failing test classes with one shared cause, reactive pipelines or timeouts, a changed model that several components disagree on, a migration, a native-image or build-configuration problem. Needs real investigation.

veryhard.describe: Concurrency, races, deadlocks, flaky or load-dependent or order-dependent failures, memory leaks, or a change that breaks the build across dozens of files (a public interface or generics refactor). Needs deep reasoning and wide edits.
